Myopia management

Myopia management uses special lenses designed to slow how quickly a child's nearsightedness progresses.

What is myopia?

Myopia, or nearsightedness, means things up close look clear but things far away look blurry. It usually happens because the eye grows too long from front to back, so light focuses in front of the retina instead of on it. Myopia often starts in childhood and can progress as children grow.

Why it matters

Myopia is more than needing stronger glasses every year. As a nearsighted eye grows longer, the tissues inside it can stretch and become thinner. Higher levels of myopia increase the risk of serious eye problems later in life, including:

  • Retinal tears and retinal detachment
  • Myopic macular degeneration, damage to the center of the retina
  • Glaucoma
  • Cataracts at a younger age

The more myopia progresses, the higher these risks become. That's why slowing it down in childhood matters.

Two options for slowing myopia

We offer two options, both FDA-authorized to slow myopia in children:

  • MiSight 1 day contact lenses (CooperVision): soft daily disposable contacts. In 2019 they became the first contact lens FDA-approved to slow myopia progression in children who start wearing them between ages 8 and 12. In the clinical study, children wearing MiSight had about 59% less progression in their glasses prescription over three years than the study's control group, who wore regular daily contacts. Like other contact lenses, MiSight carries a risk of eye infection. See our contact lens page.
  • Essilor Stellest eyeglass lenses: in 2025 these became the first eyeglass lenses FDA-authorized to slow myopia progression in children who start wearing them between ages 6 and 12. The lens has a clear center for sharp vision, surrounded by rings of tiny lenslets. In the two-year clinical study, children wearing Stellest had about 71% less progression in their glasses prescription than the study's control group, who wore regular single-vision glasses.

These results come from separate studies and do not directly compare the two treatments. We evaluate each child to determine which option may be appropriate.

These are average results from the studies. Every child responds differently, and neither option can reverse myopia that's already there. We'll check your child's eyes regularly to see how their myopia is changing. Learn about children's eye exams.
